entities.summary:
Diether von Isenburg (died May 16, 1482) was a pivotal figure in the complex ecclesiastical and political landscape of 15th-century Germany, serving twice as Archbishop-Elector of Mainz. His tenure, marked by significant conflict with both papal and imperial authorities, underscored the shifting power dynamics within the Holy Roman Empire during its late medieval phase. As an Elector, he wielded immense influence over imperial succession, while his role as metropolitan bishop positioned him at the heart of German church administration and intellectual life, notably through his founding of the University of Mainz in 1477. His career encapsulates the persistent tensions between territorial princely power, imperial prerogative, and papal supremacy that characterized the era.

First elected Archbishop of Mainz in 1459, Diether immediately clashed with Pope Pius II over the confirmation fees (annates) and his reformist demands, which challenged established papal fiscal practices. This dispute escalated into the Mainz Diocesan Feud (1461-1462), a bloody conflict that saw him excommunicated by Pius II and deposed in favor of Adolf II of Nassau. Diether's forces were decisively defeated at the Battle of Pfeddersheim, leading to his temporary exile and the loss of his see. However, following Adolf II's death in 1475, Diether was remarkably re-elected and reinstated as Archbishop in 1476, having reconciled with the papacy and Emperor Frederick III, demonstrating his enduring political acumen and local support.
